subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNISTIC ATTITUDE OF CERTAIN FOREIGN-LANGUAGE NEWSPAPERS
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) based upon a press report dated yesterday of a statement made by Professor Watson Kirkconnell of McMaster university to the effect that fifth-column activity in Canada is serious. I quote the article:
Giving what he described as examples of communist publications now appearing in Canada, Doctor Kirkconnell said there was a Hungarian-language weekly newspaper published in Toronto which "put on a chameleon act and emerged as a 100 per cent democratic paper" after the communist party was outlawed.
"The technique employed was to substitute the word 'Democracy' for the word 'Communism' in its columns and carry on much as before". The paper is "obviously Communist in sympathy", Dr. Kirkconnell said and "is still able to carry on in the heart of Toronto because it has found a formula that pays lip service to democracy."
Dr. Kirkconnell said there was a Ukrainian paper published in Smoky Lake, Alta.
"With consummate cleverness, every item of news or editorial opinion is conducive to a communist point of view in its reader."
The great majority in each group of European Canadians is loyal to Canada and their foreign-language press has rendered invaluable service to Canada, Dr. Kirkconnell said.
Will the minister have this statement investigated, and, if he finds the facts are as stated, take appropriate action to have these papers suppressed?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour based on a report in the Toronto Telegram of May 22. It states:
Six hundred employees of the Canadian Acme Screw and Gear Company, Limited, walked out on strike to-day from the company's Weston Road plant.
Ninety-five per cent of the firm's work is in the interest of Canadian and British war production.
The report goes on to say:
The company has already appealed to the authorities at Ottawa in connection with the stoppage of work on the war contracts and a representative of the dominion's Department of Labour is conferring with the management and the workers.
In view of the seriousness of the stoppage of work at this plant, would the minister care to make a statement?

In presenting the post office estimates for the consideration of the committee, I wish to point out that the requirements for 1941-42 show an increase of $1,923,942.50, or approximately 4-96 per cent over the appropriation in the main estimates for 1940-41. It is also desirable to direct the attention of the committee to the postal revenue for the year 1940-41, and I may be permitted to quote figures as regards gross receipts, which constitute the standard for measuring increased volume of mail.
Gross revenue for 1940-41, subject to final verification, shows an increase of over $3,649,900 compared with 1939-40, or an increase of 8-25 per cent. As pointed out on more than one occasion by my predecessors, increases in postal revenue must necessarily be reflected in increased expenditures under such headings as salaries of post office staffs to handle mail, printing and stationery and other supplies used in postal work, as well as conveyance of mail by railway and steamboat. Further, in times like the present, the department must expect to pay higher prices for mail services which have to be readvertised. It does not seem unreasonable that the Post Office Department should require an increase of less than three per cent in appropriation in view of the increase of more than eight per cent in gross revenue in 1940-41.

With regard to
the increase of S13,000 in publicity and advertising, why should the postal department have to publicize itself?

The increase in this vote will be sufficient to enable the department

to carry out a modest programme of general postal publicity. It is essential and in keeping with sound business practice to advertise the various regular postal services and facilities to Canadian business men and the public in time of war as well as in time of peace. During a period of hostilities unusual conditions arise which call for changes in the service and special provision to handle the postal business of the public. It is necessary to keep the public adequately informed on such matters. Further, it is felt that the $47,000,000 revenue of the post office should be protected by publicity. The appropriation requested, $20,000, represents less than one-half of one per cent of the departmental turnover. The Bell Telephone company advertise practically continuously; the Ontario hydro electric commission advertises, as do other utilities. The business of the Post Office Department is not restricted to the handling of letters. During last year we did upwards of $173,000,000 in money order business and $14,000,000 in postal note business. These are just two of the items. We have a business turnover of approximately $1,000,000 per day, which is quite a large volume of business.

Has the Postmaster
General made any provision for extension of the postal service in the urban area immediately adjacent to the city of Ottawa? I think it is well within his knowledge that within the last year or so there has been a great increase in population, particularly in the Westboro area, Laurentian View and Hilson avenue districts. Last Christmas there was serious congestion in the postal services for that area, the mail being delayed anywhere from five to fifteen days. I am pleased to report that in pursuance of a request made to the department, certain investigations of the facilities in this area have been made, and I understand it was recommended by the officials that five additional carriers be appointed for this area. The situation calls, I think, for the establishment of a postal terminal there. An extension of rural mail delivery in certain sections would also greatly facilitate postal deliveries. Has any appropriation been made to improve the postal service in that area, particularly in the rush period at Christmas? I hope that action will be taken before the next Christmas rush comes on.
I am much obliged to the officials of the department and to the Postmaster General for the courtesies I have always received at their hands, but I am again bringing this matter to the attention of the minister in the hope that provision will be made in the estimates for improving this service.

I can assure the hon. member that this matter is receiving the earnest consideration of the officials of the department and no doubt they will bring it to my attention, especially in view of the hon. member's remarks this afternoon. I cannot, of course, give him any assurance until I learn just what the facts are, but I shall be glad to look into the matter in the very near future.

I am sure the minister is delighted with the rapidity with which his items are passing. I wish to bring to his attention what may seem to be a small matter, but in my judgment it is an important one. If this is not the right item upon which to bring the matter up, or if I am not addessing myself to the right department I trust the minister will bear with me and bring my observations to the attention of the proper authority.
The hon. member for Churchill not being here at the moment I want to say a word on behalf of this outpost of Canada, the port of Churchill on Hudson bay. Early in August of this year, as has been done for I have forgotten just how many years, an excursion will be run to Churchill by the Canadian National Railway. A large proportion of those who go on this excursion are from the United States, the purpose being to bring into the country United States dollars. I understand that the excursion is going to be run again this year. I went on it myself last year, and I must say I had difficulty in finding the post office at Churchill. I am not finding fault with anyone there because they were all very courteous-
Do not advertise Churchill post office.

I can advertise the
courteousness of the post office officials, anyway. They were just what the Postmaster General would wish for in the way of courteousness and kindliness. But the post office facilities were altogether inadequate, and the building itself could be made more attractive. It struck me that visitors from the United States, wandering up to this little post office, would think, "This is the kind of postal service Canada supplies at one of its ports"-not knowing, of course, that a train runs to Churchill only once every two weeks, or even less frequently. I thought it was my duty to bring the matter to the minister's attention to see if something could not be done to brighten up that little office so that a Canadian visiting it amongst all these citizens of the United States would be proud of it. I myself sent out three or four hundred postcards and letters from the post office when I was there. I wanted my constituents back home, of course, to know that I was on the job, and the Americans were making a large use of the post office too. On many occasions there would be about a dozen people trying to get into the little building. This is no reflection on the postal officials there, because they really deserved credit for being able to do what they did do. But for the sake of the country at large may I suggest that the post office at Churchill be brightened up before the next Canadian National excursion of this year, so that our United States cousins will find an attractive little post office in this out-of-the-way locality.
Supply-Post Office
I thank the hon. member for Davenport for bringing this matter to my attention. I shall be glad to have a report made immediately on the postal facilities at Churchill.

The department has an increased amount for advertising this year. It seems to me that the post office savings bank should be used much more extensively, and some money might be spent in advertising it. I am surprised at the large number of Canadians who have no knowledge that the post office carries this banking service. I have never seen any advertisement of it. Will any part of the advertising appropriation be used to promote the use of the post office savings bank?

The assistant deputy has just advised me that he has not available at the moment the figures with respect to the post office savings bank, but I shall be glad to give them to my hon. friend upon some other item. There have recently been substantial withdrawals from the post office savings bank because people have been investing their money in war savings certificates and government bonds. I shall bear in mind what the hon. member suggests with regard to advertising the savings bank. As a matter of fact it is one of the things we do advertise, but we have such a small appropriation for advertising that it has been difficult to carry out a proper advertising campaign, particularly in view of the necessity for considerable advertising of changes in service, proper addressing of letters for overseas, and so forth. Of course any advertising has to be dominion-wide, and the hon. member will agree that S50,000 is a modest sum for advertising. Of that amount $20,000 is in this general item and $30,000 in the air mail item. So that the department have not been able to spread itself in advertising; but I shall be glad to bear in mind my hon. friend's representations.

Could the minister give information as to the amount on deposit in the post office savings account, and some comparison with the amount of money on deposit in the savings bank accounts of the chartered banks of Canada?
That comes under item 246.

I should like a little more information from the minister with respect to Saturday afternoon deliveries. First of all, I commend him for having remembered my inquiry on a previous occasion with respect to this matter. It does not affect business people so much as householders who 
require their letters, papers and periodicals over the week-end. While complimenting the minister upon endeavouring to save $300,000 in expenditures, I should like a little more information as to how this saving is effected. I assume that these mail carriers are employed by the week. The interests of the householder should be paramount to the interests of the mail carrier, although we are all, I believe, in sympathy with the mail carriers; for most of them, at least in my part of the country, are courteous and perform splendid service in carrying on their work. How is this $300,000 saved with respect to these mail carriers, who ordinarily should deliver the mail Saturday afternoon as well as Friday afternoon?

Our letter carriers are on a forty-four hour week. If there were a Saturday afternoon service, and it were operated by the same staff, it would mean a forty-eight hour week; and in order to give service in that extra four hours a proportionate increase in the number of the staff would be necessary, the cost of which has been worked out at approximately $300,000. As a matter of fact, because of the increase of business, the increased cost would probably be, the officials advise me, in the neighbourhood of $325,000 at the present time.

I often visit various places in my riding where stamps and other postal supplies are sold, and in the main I find such places quite satisfactory; but occasionally, without finding any fault with those who handle the affairs of the department, I have wondered if conditions could not be improved with a view of obtaining more revenue. As we all know, the postal department is one department, if not the only one, which really turns in money to the treasury over and above the cost of operation. Is it the only department, Mr. Chairman?
There is the Department of National Revenue.

I had not in mind national revenue; its business is to collect revenue.
I was referring to operating departments. What struck me on various occasions, particularly in visiting these small branch offices-I do not mean those belonging to the department-
Revenue post offices.

-was, whether an effort could not be made to attract the attention of the public to opportunities of saving by sending parcels by parcel post; also, when

Supply-Post Office
sending money, whether they could not be induced to buy postal notes instead of purchasing bank notes or express orders. Increased transportation of parcels and sales of money orders would bring revenue to the country's own business. I believe that if a survey were made it would be found that, in these two particulars, many of these small post offices in stores and other places of business do not sufficiently present to the public the facilities offered by the department.
Again, while in most places the accommodation is satisfactory, I have found others where it was a job to get in to buy stamps, and if two or three people happen to go there at one time they are kept waiting so long that they go away.

That is one of the reasons why we wanted an increase in the vote for advertising. I am glad to have in this matter the support of the hon. member for Davenport. We have been doing quite a lot in the way of preparing small cards and paper advertising right in our own offices in the Langevin block. It is being done in an economical manner and is working out most satisfactorily. We intend to continue advertising the business of this department, and it is a great thing to know we have in this respect the support of the hon. member for Davenport, if not of the hon. member for St. Paul's.

It would be interesting
to me, and I am sure, to the public, to know what has been the revenue during the past year, first, from the sale of stamps; second, the sale of postal notes; third, parcel post operations.

I believe that would come more
appropriately under item
With the permission of the hon. member, I will answer a little later.

2ff3. Inspection and investigation, $934,255.

What exactly does the
inspection cover?

The details are at page 156 of the
estimates.
There is a small increase.

No; I was not inquiring
about the increases. I wish to know something about the efficient work this staff is doing.

They carry on the general
inspection work of the whole postal service 14873-196
from coast to coast. In the event of shortages, loss of mail, theft, disappearance of articles, or the destruction by fire of anything in transit, the inspection staff is available to make a thorough investigation into the circumstances, and to report. The headquarters of the service is, of course, in Ottawa, under Mr. Fortier. We have found them to be most efficient, and I believe they are doing excellent work for the department. I do not know that anything unusual has happened this year, excepting that, with the increased volume of business, more demands have been made upon them.

It is marvellous what the post office officials can do when a letter is misdirected. I am speaking of the great city of Toronto, and I have had occasion to check on it. How they are able to ascertain what has happened to a letter posted in a box in my community I cannot understand, but they are able to trace that letter and give a report with regard to it. It is marvellous. It is interesting to watch the operations of the department and to observe the way in which they detect things. The postal staff in this connection is a credit to the country.

Is the directory service furnished only in the large cities, or is it limited to cities of a certain size? The service given in Calgary is very much appreciated, and yet I have had one or two criticisms. I have never been able to understand why, if an address is improperly given on a letter addressed to some city or town, it is returned to the sender without any effort to locate the addressee of the letter. Has the department a definite policy in that regard?
A certain matter was brought to my attention at Christmas, and I was interested in a report published with reference to the saving of foreign exchange which has been effected by the Post Office Department through the detection of attempts on the part of Canadians to forward American currency to the United States. I know of three or four instances in which, thanks to an extremely efficient branch of the service, considerable foreign exchange was saved. I believe the amount ran into hundreds of thousands of dollars during the past year. Has the minister any information in that respect?

With regard to the first question, about five per cent of the letters go through a small staff which is engaged in each of the large cities to deal with improperly addressed mail. The percentage may vary, but that is the approximate average. Every endeavour is made to locate the correct address.



Supply-Post Office
I hope the hon. member will not ask too many details about the manner in which we check on foreign exchange.
I am not asking how it is done.

We prefer not to give such details, but I can assure the committee that substantial amounts have been detected and reported to the foreign exchange control board for such action as they deem it proper to take. Item agreed to.

Does this item cover the salaries of all those associated with the railway mail service?
Yes.
Does the vote cover payments made for ocean carriage?
Yes.
What arrangements are made to determine how much is owing to other countries in connection with the transport of mail?

One of the hon. members representing Vancouver asked me to get some information as to the arrangements we had made in the Atlantic and Pacific services. The hon. member is interested in transit rates, which is one of the most complicated matters in the whole department. I could talk for some time, and I am quite sure that if I read the particulars he would have as much difficulty in understanding the matter as I should have in explaining it. If he would come over to the department I would take him to an authority on the subject, but I suggest that he had better set aside a day or so, because it is a highly complicated matter.
How much is paid to each of the railways?

The payments are, for
1939-40: Canadian National Railways $3,042,620.06; Canadian Pacific Railway, $3,601,491.06; other lines, $334,614.79, or a total of $6,978,725.91.
Has the minister the figures for 1940-41?
They are not yet available.
On what basis is the determination arrived at as between the two railways for the handling of mails?

The basic consideration is how the public can best be served. One matter to which I would call the hon. member's attention is the fact that the line from Montreal 
to Vancouver on the Canadian Pacific runs through the southern part of the country, whereas the Canadian National runs through the northern part. We have railway post offices, postal cars which are used for sorting purposes, and these are sent through to the more thickly populated districts. They are expensive but necessary to give service and to expedite the handling of mail. Such a car starts from Montreal, say, loaded, and, as it proceeds west, the bags of mail are dealt with and put off at different points. That space is then available and is used to pick up more mail bags. Mail has been diverted and sent so that that space may be used and that mail car will not proceed largely empty while the department is at the same time paying for space in another car. That is one of the large amounts.

I understand that the Canadian National running in the northern part of the country and the Canadian Pacific running in the southern part would distribute mail to the smaller places along their lines, but if I drop a letter in a box in Toronto for Winnipeg it could go equally well by either railway. What is the determining factor? Is it split fifty-fifty, or how?

My official advises me that it depends to a great extent upon the time that letter is posted; when it is collected and sorted; it is distributed according to the train which will give the better service. Mail between those points is sent by both railways.
Is this estimate increased or decreased from last year?
It is increased.

This is not a grant to the railways. We pay for the space we occupy in those cars for the handling of the mail.
But there was approximately $3,000,000 paid to each railway. Was that an increase over last year or a decrease?
An increase.

How would that be arrived at. It would not be according to the number of pounds of mail or the number of letters, because the minister says

Supply-Post Office
they pay according to the space occupied. Why, then, would there be an increase or a decrease?
We had a great deal more business this year than the year before and needed more space.

In connection with the division of the business between the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, the figures given by the minister show that the Canadian Pacific gets a good deal more money. I believe the Canadian National has a considerably larger mileage in Canada than the Canadian Pacific. The answer given to the hon. member for Weyburn is, I think, not satisfactory. As I understand, a train on each railway leaves Toronto at the same time and arrives in Winnipeg at the same time. The same thing applies coming east; two trains leave Winnipeg within fifteen minutes of each other and arrive at Toronto at the same time. What is the policy followed in deciding whether mail will be carried by Canadian National or Canadian Pacific, and why does the Canadian National not receive a larger share of the revenue in view of the fact that it has a much larger number of employees and a much greater mileage in Canada?

It comes back to what I said at first. The Canadian Pacific has the southern route through the west and runs through the larger centres of population. What the post office is interested in is giving service to the public. We could not send the mail up to the north line and then bring it down south; we want it on the through line. In the maritimes my understanding is that the great volume of business goes to the Canadian National. It is a matter of the best service.

I was not suggesting that the mail from Calgary to Toronto should be carried by the Canadian National, or that the mail from Saskatoon should be carried by the Canadian Pacific. It is obvious that mail from points on a main line should be carried on that main line. There are, however, two main lines between Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal, both good lines giving good service. What we wish to find out is how it is decided whether that mail will be carried by Canadian National or Canadian Pacific, and whether there is any reason why the Canadian National should not have a larger share of the business.
All of it.

I would not go that far, because places served by the Canadian 14873-196i
Pacific must have mail. Where, however, the two lines compete, the Canadian National certainly should have their fair share. I do not suggest they should have all, but they should have the bulk of it. According to the information the minister has given, they are not getting a square deal.

I wish to compliment the department if they are dividing the mail on a fair basis between the two roads. The hon. member evidently does not know that the great west country from which he comes was opened up by the Canadian Pacific and that that railway was largely responsible for the great advancement of those four western provinces. They are both great roads, and for my part I am in favour of that kind of business being split between them.
The Canadian Pacific has been well paid for its service.

I am not complaining about the business being divided, but I wish to know why the Canadian National is not getting a fair share, and I would say that a fair share would be in proportion to the mileage. The Canadian National has more employees and a much greater mileage.

The business is not
divided on the basis of mileage; it is distributed on the basis of population centres through which the railway goes and the service that the railways can give to the post office so that the post office in turn may give the best service to the public. The hon. member may be quite confident that I shall be delighted to go into this matter fully and see to it that there is no discrimination of any kind against the Canadian National Railways in the handling of our mail. On the other hand, as I think the hon. member admitted a moment ago, he would not, I believe, wish the department to show undue discrimination against the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Which is our largest
taxpayer.

I still have not had an answer to my question. My point is that there is discrimination against our own railway, according to these figures; and I must repeat that the minister has not given any information as to the policy followed in distributing the business between points such as Winnipeg and Toronto or Winnipeg and Montreal, where you have similar services. There is no question about the population or the train services, and we would like to know the policy followed in distributing business.
Supply-Post Office

The officials advise me that if a mail leaving Winnipeg is going by connecting lines which are Canadian Pacific, it goes Canadian Pacific; if it is going by connecting lines that are Canadian National, it goes Canadian National, and the business is divided up.

I am still waiting for an answer as to the policy followed in regard to letters mailed in Winnipeg for delivery in Montreal or Toronto. How does the department determine over which line they are to be sent? It is perfectly clear that letters originating at Canadian National points will go by Canadian National, and vice versa; but what is the policy followed in connection with through mail?
Both railways are used, of course.

Has the minister any
information as to what proportion of the transatlantic mail has been lost? I carry on a fairly steady correspondence to and fro, and I am astonished at the very small quantity of mail that apparently is lost, having regard to the dangers through which it has to pass. It would be very interesting if the minister could give us some information as to the losses.

I hesitate to give any
figures of losses, but I would say they have been very small.
I am not asking for the definite figures, but perhaps the minister could give us the proportion.

On the whole we have been very fortunate in connection with the loss of mail. I should be glad to show the hon. member the figures in confidence, but I think he will agree that it might be better not to place them on Hansard.

I was not asking for
definite figures. I thought it might be of general interest if some sort of proportion could be given, but if the minister prefers not to give it I am quite satisfied.

The losses have been
remarkably small.

Item agreed to.
245. Air and land mail services, $11,514,882.

I notice a considerable
increase in this item, and particularly an increase in the amount for mail service on land, including rural mail delivery. Is this an added service, or does it represent an increase in the number of rural mail delivery contracts? I believe a great many of these 
rural mail contracts are let at amounts far below what would be reasonable and right. For years many of these contractors have been carrying mail for altogether too little, and under present conditions I do not believe they are getting anything like what they should. Has there been any increase in the rural mail service? How many contracts have been readvertised and how many renewed, and have any been renewed at higher rates without tenders being called? I believe there is a great deal of valuable information that might be given in connection with the rural mail service.
While I am on my feet, will the minister give the reason for the very considerable increase, from $8,800 to $30,000, for publicity; and for the increase of $17,000 in the amount for rural mail delivery boxes?

To deal first with the question of publicity, this vote has to do with air and land mail services, and this increased amount devoted to publicity is almost entirely in connection with the air mail.
As to the rural mail delivery, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle knows, this is one of the most difficult questions with which the Post Office Department has had to contend, under all postmasters general, for many years past. I realize that in some instances the rural mail carriers find it difficult to get along at present rates. In the past I have discussed from time to time suggestions that have been made by representatives of the rural mail carriers' association, and I believe that at the present time they do not feel this matter should be opened up. They do not wish to come out for a general upward revision, with the war on and conditions as they are; they feel that perhaps this would be a most inopportune time to ask for a change. My officials advise me that figures are not available at the moment giving the number of contracts advertised and renewed, though I may be able to get the information for the hon. member. The hon. gentleman also asked as to renewals at higher prices, but I can assure him that so far as I know there have been none. I understood the hon. member to ask in regard to contracts which had been renewed at higher prices without being advertised.
No, the number readvertised at higher prices.

I have not that information. I thought the hon. member referred to contracts renewed at higher rates, without having been advertised.

Supply-Post Office
By any chance could the minister give us the number of renewals by constituencies?
I am sorry I cannot give that information.

I was greatly impressed by the apparent growth of the air mail service, which was brought out in the evidence given before the railway committee a few days ago. I was particularly interested because of the improved service which has been given us in the maritimes. If I remember correctly it was about the middle of March when certain members from Nova Scotia applied to the Postmaster General for a more satisfactory service, and about April 15 we were given that service. Now, instead of an uncertain daily service we are given two services a day.
Following the inauguration of this improved service some question was raised as to whether the government was wise in cancelling the contract held by Canadian Airways and entering into a new agreement with Trans-Canada Air Lines. I should like some information from the Postmaster General in connection with the new contract so that I may be in position intelligently to meet the criticism that has been offered from time to time in the maritimes about this particular item. What has been the profit or loss on the carrying of air mail between Halifax and Moncton by Canadian Airways? What is the present situation as to profit and loss, now that Trans-Canada Air Lines has taken over the service? Has there been any improvement since Trans-Canada Air Lines started operations?
We appreciate the improvements which have been made, and we are satisfied that the Post Office Department is doing everything it can to give us good service. It is true that for a long time the department did not seem to know that Halifax existed. I asked repeatedly why Halifax did not appear on the maps which were published year after year. After a long wait we are at last able to say "thank you" to the Post Office Department for this service.

The old service was
operated by Canadian Airways at a daily cost of S136.80. The total distance was 114 miles, that is once each way, at 60 cents. The average daily poundage of mail from Halifax was 51, and the estimated revenue attributable to air mail service was S102. This was made up of 51 pounds of mail, at 50 letters to the pound, at four cents per letter, not taking all of the six cents. There was an estimated daily deficit of $34.80. Under the new service operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines the daily
cost is $212.40 for a two-trip service with a larger plane. The estimated revenue attributable to air mail service is $234, made up of 117 pounds, at 50 letters to the pound, at four cents per letter. There is an estimated daily surplus of $21.60.

There is a difference of
approximately $55 a day due to improved service. I repeat that we appreciate what has been done in this regard; it demonstrates that it pays to put on an improved service so far as the maritimes are concerned.
I suggest that in all future literature or maps the name of Halifax be shown.

I should like to say a word or two on behalf of the underpaid rural mail carriers. I realize that this is not the time to put forward a plea on behalf of any individual district, but the conditions which prevail in my district are to be found in many other areas where the climatic conditions are similar. There are a great many rural mail carriers in the Parry Sound district, and I have personally investigated most of their contracts. As they have matured and have been renewed I have had to do with them. The mail remuneration for carrying long distances over difficult roads is really pitiful.
Unfair.

And it becomes unfair. I want to record my views now, even though I am not suggesting in this year of financial stress that this is the time to raise rates. But the moment this unhappy war is over it is one of the first reforms that we as a self-respecting country ought to bring about. We should give these men a remuneration that compensates them for their responsible and arduous duties.
Can the hon. member give the committee any information as to the amount of mail that the citizens of Parry Sound receive once every five years?

My hon. friend's well known quality of submerging barbs in honeyed words has not failed him on this occasion. But let me tell him that a comparison of the grades of the scholars in the schools of Windsor with the grades of the scholars in the schools of Parry Sound will indicate that two letters are written or received by the citizens and children of Parry Sound for every one written or received by the constituents of my hon. friend.
That is not Windsor.

I am not including the prolific mail which the five young ladies at Callander receive. But to get back to the conditions facing these rural mail carriers who
Supply-Post Office

must battle with the elements: I know of one route twenty-one miles in length where in winter the depth of snow ranges from six to eight feet over most of the route. A car simply cannot go through, and the carrier must have a team of horses for the winter season and a car for the rest of the year. In my district, as in many others, the great tradition that his majesty's mail must go through is lived up to by these men who are serving the country. But their contracts show an actual loss at the end of the season. When the proper opportunity comes this should be one of the first reforms put into effect.

In referring to the air mail service the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) apparently spoke for the maritimes. I have no doubt that much improvement has been made in the service rendered the city of Halifax, but to many other parts of the province the extension of that service is of very little benefit. It takes more time to send a letter by air mail to the part of the country from which I come than it does to send it by ordinary post. The air mail must be unloaded at Moncton and transferred to a plane for Halifax, whence it goes by train to its destination. When in April the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) was piloting a bill through the house having to do with Trans-Canada Air Lines, he said that no place in Canada would benefit more largely by an extension of air mail and passenger service than Sydney, Nova Scotia, and that it was the intention to have the present condition remedied this summer. I notice that this appropriation has been increased by $651,006. If it is necessary to provide a subsidy in order to extend this air service, has the Post Office Department budgeted for such a subsidy, and is it included in this vote?

This is a matter I should like to discuss with my colleague, the Minister of Munitions and Supply, before making any statement. There are funds in this vote for extensions of air service at necessary points, but I can make no definite statement at the moment as to dates or locations, because that depends upon many circumstances. I should not be surprised if there were some changes in the maritime area, but it is a matter of policy I must discuss with my colleague.

If a subsidy had been budgeted for, the minister would likely know about it. There has been continuous correspondence over the last year between the people of the island of Cape Breton and the government with reference to the establishment of both

mail and passenger service. I think the government recognizes the necessity for such a service. We are living in an obsolete and out-of-the-way part of the country down there, lacking up-to-date transportation facilities, and the Minister of Munitions encouraged me greatly, when piloting his bill through, by definitely stating that conditions would be remedied this summer. Better facilities are anxiously awaited, but the fact that the Postmaster General and his department are not aware of any subsidy being appropriated for the purpose would rather lead me to believe that nothing is being done.

I am afraid the hon.
member misunderstood me. There is money available under certain circumstances for extensions of service, but the question of equipment and personnel must be considered. I can assure the hon. member that the matter is receiving consideration. I do not want him to think for a moment that it has been lost sight of, but without consulting my colleague I cannot give him a definite statement as to when the matter will be decided.
I understood that equipment and personnel had already been taken care of, and that all that was necessary before an extension of service could be made, was a subsidy.

I should like to support the plea made by the hon. member for Parry Sound on behalf of the rural mail carriers. Early consideration should be given to this matter. Rural mail carriers should not have to wait until after the war for the necessary increase in their remuneration. What they receive now is a disgrace. I know one rural mail carrier who travels twenty-eight miles every day and receives a dollar a day. Surely some consideration should be given to the men who take these contracts to keep off relief. Their expenses now are much higher than they were. I hope the minister will give this matter his early consideration.

Under the law as it now
exists, the minister is required to call for tenders and the contract is awarded to the lowest tenderer, unless for some special reason a man is unable or unfit to perform the service. The difficulty is that some of the tenders are so low, as the hon. member for Parry Sound and other members have mentioned, that in some instances hardships are bound to be caused. After all, in some cases the man has put in a low tender in order to get the contract from somebody else. It is a difficult matter to deal with. One suggestion that has been made is that all the carriers should

Supply-Post Office
keep their present routes at an increased rate; on the other hand, others have tendered at a lower figure than even that increased rate, and it would be unfair to them. If you established a fixed rate you would also have this difficulty, that probably twenty or thirty people in certain districts would apply for the rural mail contract over the same route and the Postmaster General would have a great deal of trouble in deciding between them. So that the difficulty is not so easily overcome as some might' think.
If hon. members have any suggestions as to how conditions could be improved, I shall appreciate it if they write to us. I can assure them that their representations will receive the most careful consideration. Not only the minister but the officials of the department as well would be delighted if somebody could find some way of improving present conditions.
If the minister could tell us the percentage of renewals at the old rate we would have some idea of what the rural carriers themselves think about it.
I shall be glad to get that information for the hon. member. I can say offhand that a very large number wish to renew their contracts at the existing rates.
And resent it greatly when they are undercut.
Some of them, yes.

Is it not true that specific performance is required of these rural mail
carriers?
Sureties.
Has there been any default and recourse to the sureties under their bonds?
Yes; in some instances the sureties have been required to carry on the route where the carrier left the district or failed to carry out the contract.
Do the sureties carry on the route or make good the default by the payment of money?
They are responsible for the performance. They are not simply recommending such and such a man as a good fellow, but are responsible for the service being carried on.
What is the penalty in the bond? Is it a monetary sum? Surely it would not be specific performance?
If the service falls down and we have to have it carried on at a higher rate, the surety is responsible for the difference in the rate.
Has recovery been made on such bonds? Has any suit been taken to recover?

Not so far as I know.
None has been brought to my attention.

To my mind we have under discussion this afternoon one of our most important services. For my part, speaking on behalf of my constituency, and, I am sure, for the people of the west, I appreciate the fact that we have as Postmaster General a young man with progressive and aggressive ideas. Nothing delighted me more than to observe the increased appropriation for advertising. I believe that the full value of the service which this department is capable of rendering to the people of Canada is not yet generally appreciated. We are now adopting modern merchandising methods in selling to the people a really worth-while service, one which has an important contribution to make to the amenities of modern life. I was interested to note that the Minister of Labour, in his announcement a few days ago, indicated that the services of the Post Office Department were to be made use of in the introduction of the unemployment insurance scheme. That is very commendable enterprise on the part of a former postmaster general who is no doubt aware of the services which that department can render to him in his new capacity of Minister of Labour.
All of us, and in particular the people of the west, appreciate what the air mail service means in monetary saving. In my firm the savings amount to hundreds of dollars in the course of a year. My professional practice is such that these savings are multiplied, and I know the same is true of the grain trade, who now use the air service in preference to the telephone and the telegraph.
Another respect in which the service is worth while is its tendency to eliminate the great blank space which exists between eastern and western Canada, and to provide another means of bringing us closer together, making for better understanding, and enabling us quickly to solve our difficulties.
I appreciate the work of the Post Office Department in this time of war. It is not easy to estimate what it means to be able to get a letter within four or five days from our dear ones and those who are close to us in England, and to be able to reply to them as rapidly. In that respect may I pay tribute to the director of postal services at Calgary. I believe that at the beginning of the war he came to Ottawa and carried out a very difficult task so well that he was sent over-
Supply-Post Office

seas and is now doing a very worth-while job over there. I have nothing but praise for the department at this time.
I see that by reducing rates on money orders and notes, a branch which was losing money for years is now showing a profit. Were we to apply to all our other services, in the same degree, modern business and merchandising methods, it would be all to the good.

I am sure that the officials of the department appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary West.
In regard to unemployment insurance, we are taking over the sale of unemployment insurance stamps under the act and thus cooperating with the Department of Labour. The department is paying us $171,000 for looking after that work for the first year; thereafter the rate, subject to revision on the basis of whether it is fair or not, will be about -57 of the cost for handling the sales of stamps and the distribution throughout Canada. This provides an outlet through 12,557 post offices throughout the country. I understand that the rate charged by the post office in Great Britain for this service is -5 per cent. Bearing in mind the fact that our area is so much greater in extent, I believe our rate is reasonable.
May I express my thanks to postmasters throughout the country for the work they have done, mostly without remuneration, to help in Canada's war effort. They have assisted freely in the war savings stamps campaign as part of their help in the service of the country. I have here a letter from the financial superintendent, Mr. H. E. Atwater, advising me as to the distribution of war savings stamps through the post offices, and it is to be noted that the sales more than doubled after the start of the war savings campaign. The letter concludes :	[DOT]
This makes a total for the post office sales of $8,757,000.
I am sure that hon. members appreciate the work that the postmasters are doing in connection with the war effort. From time to time we receive letters from postmasters authorizing deductions of salary, contributing percentages of salary, giving up certain amounts voluntarily for the duration of the war, for a year, or for a certain number of months; or applying a certain portion to the purchase of war savings certificates. We know of many such cases, and we are satisfied that postmasters will take their full part in the effort to assist the Department of Finance in the new loan. About $237,000 worth of certificates have been purchased by postmasters so far this year, and in addition there have 
been outright gifts of over a thousand dollars. A few months ago, when members of the postmasters' association came to Ottawa, they made a presentation to the Prime Minister on behalf of their association of $6,000 in stamps. We should appreciate what they are doing in this regard. Many have only small offices, and these contributions mean a good deal to them. It shows that their hearts are in the right place, and that they are doing a job for this country to the very best .of their ability.

Is it not a fact that prior to 1930 the rates received by rural mail carriers compared favourably with the post office estimates of the rates at which mail could be carried? In 1931, 1932 and 1933 the department established a practice of throwing open to tender as many routes as possible, and when times were so hard during those years people tendered for these routes at less than half of what the mail could be carried for. That accounts for the low rates which have been established for the carrying of rural mail. To-day we are asked by these mail carriers to renew their contracts, and that keeps the rates at the low standard fixed between 1930 and 1935. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) say that he lived in an obsolete part of the country. A short time ago the hon. gentleman said that Nova Scotia had gone behind fifty years. The same thought ran through my mind on the night of March 26, 1940, when news came over the radio that that province had elected a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation member.

This total vote amounts to $11,514,882. It will be found on page 28 of the estimates, the details being given on page 159. They can, however, hardly be correctly called details. During the past hour several hon. members have referred to contracts held by the majority of rural mail carriers. I believe the minister intimated that he would welcome suggestions for the correction of the existing evil, and I am going to take advantage of this opportunity to point out what I regard as a vicious practice that has grown up in connection with the rural mail carrier service. In certain distribution centres off rail, certain enterprising gentlemen, engaged in remunerative occupations, have made it a point to bid for the job of mail carrier, and owing to the fact that these men do not depend to any appreciable degree upon the revenue derived from that particular work have been able to outbid practically all others. In certain instances those who would depend upon the revenue which they would derive from the work are shut out, with the result that in one centre in particular which I have in mind one gentleman holds three contracts and engages in the practice of subletting. That is something which, in my opinion, should not be allowed. I would say, therefore, that if a man indicates his willingness to bid for the position of carrier, he ought to indicate or be compelled to indicate that he is prepared to do the work himself.
I find that in one case which I can mention -and I am willing to mention it later to the minister this gentleman has kept for himself, out of two or three contracts, approximately $50 per contract, which is clear income for him, but he has put men on the road under a subcontract system. It is almost impossible for them to carry on. Someone may say that they do not have to take the work; but if rMr. Mulock.]
to-morrow I offered a job paying $100 a year, there would certainly be someone who would find himself by force of circumstances in a position where he would be glad to accept the work. Consequently we have men carrying on this work, some of them getting $20 or $30 a month, and having ten and fifteen mile routes. I deplore the fact.
I would ask the minister to what extent his department renews contracts without advertising. Perhaps it does not do so at all. At any rate, is it the practice, and to what extent is it carried on?
There is one other matter I wish to discuss. I believe the minister stated when we were discussing administration that contracts under $200 a year are let by him-or may be let. He did not say they are let by himself, but they may be. This thought went through my mind: How many contracts that would possibly provide for the bidder $300 a year are forced down by the minister into the class of $200 a year or less, and are sublet to someone else by the successful holder? There is always someone to take such a contract if it is handed to him. I am just asking for information. I am not saying it is done;
I base my statement on the statement made by the minister.

A very large number of
contracts are renewed without being put up for further tender, if the service performed has been satisfactory. That has always been the principle followed by the department. The minister has power to authorize renewal.
I do not quite know what the hon. member objects to about this other matter; the $200 is not used to drive any one down in price.

Supply-Post Office

I am not objecting; I am
merely seeking information. The unfortunate part of there being no definite policy with regard to renewing contracts is this. A certain man comes along and underbids another by five dollars or thereabouts.
I have another definite case in this regard, a friend of mine, right after the 1935 election. The minister may draw any conclusion he likes. I doubt whether that same man has had an opportunity since 1935 to bid again, and perhaps underbid the other man. There should be a definite practice in this regard; it should not be left to the discretion of the minister or some departmental official to say, "Here we will call for tenders, and there we will give it back to the present contractor." There may be others just as much entitled and just as well qualified to carry on the work.

The splendid advance
in the air mail branch of the post office is something of which we must all feel proud. It carries mail so rapidly to remote areas and brings the different parts of the country into close contact.
Has the minister before him the weight or number of letters carried by the air mail service in Canada, and has it produced a profit or a deficit, and how much?

I have quite a long statement here. There has been a substantial increase in air mail. We have some very good officials in the department who keep in close touch with the situation and keep me in touch. I hesitate almost to rely too much upon the graphs that they prepare.
For a while we were getting an increase of about four per cent a month, about fifty per cent a year, a tremendous increase. Based on that increase, they worked out this plan, and they hope that in the near future the revenue from air mail will meet the cost that we pay to Trans-Canada Air Lines to help them operate. I understand the figures were given to the railway committee the other day. The indications are so good that I hesitate to give them. I would rather wait a few months.
Why?

Because so many things
may occur. I have the example of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) who said he is not going to make any more prophecies, so I hesitate to do so in this regard. I can say, however, that the indications are quite encouraging. For example, for February we estimated that we would have a gross weight of air mail carried of 77,952 pounds. We exceeded that and received 82,487
pounds. In March we estimated 89,745 pounds and actually received 91,453 pounds. In April we estimated 90,330 pounds and actually received 99,071 pounds. For April, the estimated difference between revenue and cost was $31,754, but with the increase in the poundage that deficit was reduced to $18,488.

The deficit is rapidly
going down?

If the present increases
are maintained, within a short time, within months at the present rate of increase, the air mail should be carrying itself. It would be a good thing if we could get it on a paying basis. That is one of the reasons why we want an increased vote for advertising. We have found the results very satisfactory; we have had satisfactory increases in the volume of air mail, and when one is dealing in millions of dollars, it seems false economy not to use a fair amount of advertising.
Do parcels going overseas to the soldiers in England take a lower rate than the regular rate?

Yes. The matter of postage on parcels for overseas is not entirely in the hands of the Postmaster General of Canada; it has to be arranged also with Great Britain. Any changes in rates must be agreed upon between the two governments. From time to time there have been suggestions of further reductions of the parcel rate, but that burden would fall to some extent on Great Britain, and we do not consider it proper to make representations for further reductions at the present time when Britain has such a great burden to carry. Yes, the postage on parcels has been reduced.

While the minister is looking up that information I should like to say that in the few remarks I made in connection with the post office estimates I endeavoured to deal as specifically as possible with the item under discussion, and I want to protest against the statements of the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Grant). I refuse to allow him to put words into my mouth. I said that I considered our end of the country obsolete so far as the services under discussion were concerned. When the hon. member made the uncalled-for statement with reference to the intelligence of the people who sent me here I think he gave a first class demonstration of his own ignorance. If I accomplish nothing more during the time I am here, at least I have given him an opportunity of getting on his feet and saying something. Perhaps the reason there are Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members in this house-

A moment ago the hon. member for Davenport asked whether the rates on soldiers' parcels had been reduced. The answer is that they have. The civilian rates are 24 cents for the first pound and 18 cents for each additional pound up to ten pounds; $2.50 for a parcel from ten pounds to fifteen pounds and S3 for a parcel from fifteen pounds to twenty pounds. In connection with parcels to soldiers the limit is eleven pounds and the rate is 12 cents per pound, for members of the British, Canadian, 
dominion or colonial troops serving in the United Kingdom.
Mr. PURDY; I wonder if some consideration might be given to allowing a leeway of a few ounces in connection with parcels going overseas. It is very annoying to reach the post office with a parcel being sent to a dear one overseas, only to find that you must go all the way back home and have your wife take out a can here or something else there because the parcel happened to be three or four ounces overweight. Could there not be some leeway in that regard?

It is not a question only of leeway on the part of our officials; it is a question of leeway on the ships, and leeway in connection with delivery in England. This question of soldiers' parcels is a matter of agreement between the postal authorities of this country and those of Britain, and we could not make any change here without the approval of the British authorities. I think the hon. member will realize that no substantial increase could be permitted. The volume of parcels is very great, and there is a limit to the amount of space available for this purpose on ships going to Britain.

But a few ounces one way or the other would not increase the size of the parcel. There should be some elasticity in the regulations to meet a situation of this kind. When you have to open a parcel and do it up all over again you sometimes miss a mail.
Mr. MULOCK. I do not think the officials would be so very difficult to deal with, but at the same time if we were to say we would permit five pound parcels to weigh up to five pounds and a half, that would soon be raised to five pounds and three-quarters, and still it would be suggested that they should be carried at the five pound rate. I am sure the officials are not unreasonable about this matter, but on the other hand you cannot say, "Yes, go ahead and make it, five and a half pounds."
I quite appreciate that, but I do dislike having to take a parcel back because it is an ounce or two overweight.

I notice in the
statement the minister was kind enough to give me that the Edmonton-White Horse service and the Vancouver-Fort St. John service both are listed as semi-weekly, and the figures in regard to their cost refer to semiweekly service. Is it not true that at the present time both these services are tri-weekly; and, if that is so, will that entail additional cost?

Questions
The hon. member is correct; these are now tri-weekly services. Certain developments taking place in that part of the country have made this desirable, as I think the hon. member will agree.
I am not objecting.
The hon. member agrees that this change was advisable?
Yes.
The moneys are available to take care of the extra services.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: INVITATION TO MEMBERS TO BE PRESENT AT MARCH PAST PEACE TOWER ON MONDAY, MAY 26
speechtext:
Perhaps the house will permit me to mention that the Lake Superior regiment, which has been in Ottawa for the last five or six weeks, is leaving the city next week and moving further east; and arrangements have been made for the regiment to march past the peace tower at 2.30 on Monday afternoon. I want to invite hon. members to be present at that time if they care to do so. It will give them an opportunity to see an excellent unit of the Canadian active army; and further it gives us an opportunity to pay a compliment to a unit which has maintained a very high standard while it has been in Ottawa.
On motion of Mr. Cirerar the house adjourned at 6 p.m.
Monday, May 26, 1941.
